newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Broaddus says U.S. economy fairly favorable.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Broaddus says U.S. economy fairly favorable.

text.p: Alfred Broaddus, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, on Thursday described the U.S. economic climate as relatively favorable.
"As far as the current economic situation is concerned, I don't see how anyone could describe it in anything other than fairly favorable terms," Broaddus told an investors group here.
He described inflation as "quite modest," emphasizing the recent trends in the so-called core Consumer Price Index, which excludes food and energy prices.
He noted that the overall CPI did "shoot up a bit" because of a temporary jump in energy prices.
Broaddus said there were some tentative signs that the economy has cooled down after robust pace of growth earlier this year.

"As we've moved past the first half of the year and the third quarter (and are) now into the fourth quarter, there are some tentative signs perhaps of some diminution in economic activity overall," he said.
While generally upbeat about the economic picture, Broaddus referred to "some evidence of some upward pressure on wages," which he said has been noticed in financial markets.
He also described labor markets as tight.

"Labor markets now -- at least according to all the information I see, not only the published statistics but the anecdotal information we get from around our district and around the country -- are already exceptionally tight," he said.
Concerning the outlook for the economy, the Richmond Fed chief said most forecasters believe that a slowdown in the economy to a more sustainable level was the most likely scenario.
He said, however, that the risks that such a slowdown might not occur in time to relieve pressure on capacity were viewed as "not negligible."
On the longer-run issue of price stability, Broaddus said the Fed still has "some distance to go" to achieve that goal.
"We're getting close but we're not there yet," he said, stressing the need to keep moving toward price stability.
Asked whether the strength of the dollar, particularly against the Japanese yen, was concerning the Fed, Broaddus said that over the longer run a strong dollar is a positive development.

"If a currency is strong over a longer period of time, it means that economic conditions in that country generally are strong or are perceived as being likely to remain strong over a period of time," Broaddus said.
